newsitem.title: USA: US aluminum premiums shoot up on nearby demand.
newsitem.headline: US aluminum premiums shoot up on nearby demand.

text.p: U.S. physical market premiums have shot up by at least a quarter of a cent per pound in the past week as metal is snapped up for first quarter deliveries, traders said.
Consumers kept their inventories low in the fourth quarter to avoid taxes, but were now looking for deliveries in January and further forward, traders said.
U.S. premiums over LME cash in the Midwest have risen to 4.50 to 5.00 cents per pound, with much of the business transacted at 4.75 cents.
Earlier this month premiums were about 4.00 to 4.25 cents.
"Premiums are going to remain strong and there is not as much Russian metal coming in because premiums in Europe and Japan have moved up too," a producer source said.

"It's just a matter of time that we get to 5.5 to 6.0 cents then all the cash and carry metal will come out of the woodwork to bring premiums down again in the second or third quarter," the source added.
Traders noted that producers have been in the market to buy and were apparently short of metal for their internal fabricating plants.

"The cash and carry guys have also been buying good healthy tonnages at these premium levels," a merchant said. "I think there will be a little bit of a crunch in January to February, but when you start to see 5.00 to 5.5 cents premiums, you get a little bit of creative importing."
Cash and carry buyers seek to snap up tonnages and use the LME contango or premium on forward months over cash to finance the storage of the metal and make a profit.

"The people doing the cash and carry consignment deals needed to buy more metal, but the customers cannot touch it yet so they also had to buy spot, which puts increased demand on the nearby market," a dealer said.
No tight shortages of metal were seen at the moment, traders said.
